title: TB1-16931
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, claims to be a citizen of Sri Lanka. He seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1.
The claimant alleges as follows:
He is a young male Tamil from Sri Lanka who was born on XXXX XXXX, 1987, in XXXX in the XXXX region.

In 2007, during large scale displacement of people in his area, the claimant was apprehended by members of the XXXX group on the way from the camp where he was staying to his parents' home. He was detained for a day and accused of being a member of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). During the detention, the claimant was interrogated and beaten. As a condition of release, he had to sign in every XXXX weeks. The claimant was warned that if he failed to sign in, he would be shot.

While attending school, the claimant lived in a different camp from where he was registered. When it was discovered by the army that the claimant was at different camp from the one at which he was registered, he was taken away and beaten. The claimant was released only after his mother pleaded with the army and was warned to remain at the camp and not attend school. The claimant was also threatened that he would be shot if it was discovered that he involved in any pro-LTTE activities. After young Tamil males started to go missing when taken for questioning, the claimant's father, fearing for the claimant's safety, made arrangements with an agent to have the claimant go to Qatar on a work permit.

In XXXX 2008, the claimant returned to Sri Lanka after finding the work in Qatar to be harder and paid at a lower rate than indicated in his contract. After arriving in Sri Lanka, the claimant was detained for three days and released after paying a sum of two lakhs for having been out of the country for some XXXX months and having failed to sign every XXXX weeks as ordered. After being released, the claimant was once again ordered to sign in every XXXX weeks. After three Sinhalese workers were shot dead in the claimant's home area in XXXX 2008, he was detained, beaten, and questioned upon arriving at the army camp to sign in.

In November 2008, three Tamils were killed by members of the army, causing the claimant to fear for his safety. Following the election in 2010, there was heightened tension, with Tamils being accused of continuing to support the LTTE. After several Tamils were shot dead, who had been signing in as had the claimant, the claimant and his family made arrangements for him to come to Canada.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee in accordance with section 96 nor a person in need of protection in accordance with section 97(1) (a) and (b) of the IRPA. ANALYSIS Identity

Several documents2 were available in support of the claimant's identity. The panel is persuaded, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is who he claims to be and is a citizen of Sri Lanka. Credibility

The claimant's testimony was generally consistent with the narrative in his Personal Information Form (PIF). The claimant, however, provided inconsistent responses as to why he had left Qatar and returned to Sri Lanka in 2008. Initially, his testimony was inconsistent with the information he gave Canadian authorities at his initial refugee claim interview, as well as the information he provided in his PIF. Only after a great deal of questioning by the both the panel and the claimant's counsel, was the claimant able to provide an answer as to why he left Qatar, that incorporated the information he provided both at the refugee claim and later in his PIF narrative.

In his initial refugee claim and application, the claimant stated: "In Qatar, since it was hard work, I wanted to continue my studies, so I returned to Sri Lanka."3 In his PIF narrative, however, the claimant indicated: "In Qatar I was not given the job as per the contract I signed. The salary was not even half of what was promised. I objected and got sent home in XXXX 2008." At the hearing, after extensive questioning, the claimant testified that he breached his contract because he was dissatisfied with the pay and hard work involved in the job. The claimant stated that he had received a letter from his employer terminating his employment at the end of the contract. He testified that he decided to return home because he had been away a long time and wanted to continue with his studies. Although the war was still going on between the Sri Lankan forces and the LTTE, the fighting was primarily in the north. According to the claimant, in his home area in the east, people were being sent home from the camps so he believed that he would face no problems in returning to Sri Lanka.

While the panel acknowledges that the claimant may simply and naively believed that he would face no problems in returning to Sri Lanka, after nearly a year's absence and after having failed to observe the conditions of his release, the panel finds his re-availment indicative of a lack of subjective fear. Well-foundedness

The claimant testified that he fears returning to Sri Lanka because he is a young Tamil from the north who was suspected of being an LTTE supporter. He also believes that he is at risk because he has been living for the past seven years in a country where the Tamil diaspora is seen by Sri Lankan authorities as being pro-LTTE. The panel has, therefore, considered if and how the claimant would fit the first risk profile as identified in the UNHCR Guidelines: "persons suspected of certain links with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE)."

The claimant's counsel, in his oral submissions, has identified a number of elements in the claimant's profile which he argues, cumulatively, indicate that the claimant will be at risk of persecution upon a return to Sri Lanka. Counsel has identified the following elements in the claimant's risk profile: * The claimant is a single Sri Lankan male who resided in the XXXX region, an area at one time under LTTE control. * He has a history of prior arrests and was suspected of being an LTTE supporter. * On returning to Sri Lanka from Canada, his travel documents would indicate that he has lived in Canada since 2011, a country where the Tamil diaspora has been viewed by the Sri Lankan government as supporters of the LTTE. * His father had provided assistance to the LTTE.

The panel has reviewed country documents with respect to problems facing Tamils in general and Tamil returnees in particular, and notes some of the key findings. The US DOS Report on Sri Lanka, for 2016, for example, states: The most significant human rights issues were included... arbitrary arrest, lengthy detention... and surveillance and harassment of civil society activists, journalists.4
In addition, members of religious minorities and persons viewed as sympathizers of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) were subjected to the aforementioned treatment.

The Amnesty International Annual Report 2017/18 on Sri Lanka found that Tamils suspected of links to the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) continued to be detained under the PTA [Prevention of Terrorism Act], which permits extended administrative detention and shifts the burden of proof onto the detainee alleging torture or other ill-treatment.5

While it is clear from the various documents referenced that those suspected of links to the LTTE face a possibility of arrest and even torture at the hands of government security forces, there are also indications that the situation is improving. Not all Tamils are routinely screened. According to research, "...only those individuals for whom the government claims there are 'reasonable concerns' of having links with the LTTE are screened."6 As well, another expert on Sri Lanka has noted that "...while those accused of links with LTTE are still 'not treated well,' the situation has 'improved a lot' since the end of the civil war [in 2009], noting that allegations of torture and detentions have diminished.

The Executive Director of the National Peace Council of Sri Lanka (NPC), has indicated that "[a]rrests and detentions are not common unless for some reasonable suspicion of criminal activities," and the President of the Council of (non-government organizations) NGOs in Sri Lanka has stated: "...arrest and detention of those with alleged links to the LTTE continue, but that they have been 'reduced' ".7 While these statements stand in contrast to some of the conclusions in other reports, the panel notes that these statements are made by individuals within the country and tend to be more recent assessments of the situation. Nonetheless, the situation in the country for Tamils, although it has improved under the current regime elected in 2015, it is far from perfect and the risk profile of an individual with suspected links to the LTTE, as identified in the UNHCR Guidelines of 2012, must be carefully considered. The panel must, therefore, determine whether the claimant faces more than a mere possibility that he will be harassed and harmed by Sri Lankan authorities upon a return to the country.

The claimant testified that he fears returning to Sri Lanka. He indicated that he will be viewed as an LTTE supporter by Sri Lankan authorities because he has lived in Canada for the past 7 years - a country where the Tamil community is seen as being pro-LTTE. The claimant was asked if, while in Canada, he had been a member/supporter of, or involved in any pro-LTTE activities, or had contributed to any pro-LTTE activities. To all these questions, the claimant replied in the negative. Later in the hearing, however, during questioning by his counsel, the claimant indicated that his father had given up his tractor to the LTTE. The panel notes that, while the claimant's father gave his tractor to the LTTE, it was done under duress. The panel finds that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the claimant's family is perceived to be supporters of the LTTE.

The panel recognizes that, despite similar general profiles, claimants' individual situations must be considered before arriving at a decision regarding the possibility of harm. The claimant alleges to have been arrested on two occasions in Sri Lanka. According to the claimant, he was apprehended by members of the XXXX paramilitary group in 2007, following "displacement of people in [his] area," because, in order to attend school, the claimant was staying at a different camp than that of his parents. The claimant stated that he was accused of being a member of the LTTE and subsequently detained for a day during which time he was beaten and tortured in an effort to have him confess to being a "Tiger." The claimant was then required to sign in every XXXX weeks. The panel finds, however, that during this critical time in the conflict between the LTTE and the Sri Lankan forces, all young male Tamils were suspected of being pro-LTTE and were targeted.

The claimant indicates that he continued to go to school, and was again detained- this time by the army for being at a camp at which he was not registered. The claimant was taken to the army camp and released only after his mother pleaded with the army to release him as he had already been beaten and question by the Karuna group and was already signing in every XXXX weeks. The army threatened to shoot him if they became aware of his involvement in any pro-LTTE activity. When Tamil youths began to "disappear" after being taken in for questioning, the claimant's father, fearing for his son's safety, arranged to have him go to Qatar on a work permit. The panel does not find that the claimant was individually targeted, but simply caught up in a general response by Sri Lankan forces to LTTE attacks and their suspicion that all young Tamils were potential members of the LTTE.

In XXXX 2008, the claimant returned to Sri Lanka after working for ten months in Qatar. When he went to the army camp to sign in, he was detained and interrogated as to why he had not signed in for nearly a year. After informing them that he had been in Qatar, they demanded money before releasing him, believing that he had made a great deal of money during his time in Qatar.

The claimant remained in Sri Lanka until November 2010, during which time he was questioned and threatened at different times, when going to sign in. When three others that had also been signing in were shot dead, the last being in October 2010, the claimant decided to flee the country.

The panel notes that the claimant's father has provided a letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018,8 stating that the army has been "checking the houses of those who left abroad." The letter indicates that they come to the father's home inquiring about the claimant's whereabouts. The letter further indicates that his father informed them that he was in Canada and that the army was suspicious as to why he was abroad.

While the letter appears to support the assertion that there continues to be interest in the claimant by authorities, the panel has considered the reliability of documentary evidence emanating from family members, and concurs with Justice Annis' view as articulated in El Bouni: ... I find that confirmatory evidence of family members and friends, which is not subject to cross-examination, is not highly probative or credible evidence. Highly probative evidence is intrinsically well-presented evidence from independent sources confirming a material fact in the matter.9 The panel also finds it curious that about a month before the claimant's hearing, the authorities would now express interest in the claimant in whom they have displayed little interest since his departure seven years ago. The panel assigns little weight to the father's letter.

The United Kingdom's (UK) Home Office Report: Country Information and Guidance. Sri Lanka: Tamil Separatism, August 2016 includes a number of significant conclusions established by the UK Tribunal in assessing recent, independent reports regarding returnees to Sri Lanka. One of the Tribunal's key findings is that: The government's present objective is to identify Tamil activists in the Diaspora who are working for Tamil separatism and to destabilise the unitary Sri Lankan state enshrined in Amendment 6(1) to the Sri Lankan Constitution in 1983, which prohibits the 'violation of territorial integrity' of Sri Lanka. Its focus is on preventing both (a) the resurgence of the LTTE or any similar Tamil separatist organisation and (b) the revival of the civil war within Sri Lanka. 10 [footnotes omitted]

The panel notes that the claimant does not have any direct ties to the LTTE, nor does he have a history of having opposed the government - either in Sri Lanka or during his time in Canada. The UK Tribunal, in assessing recent, independent reports regarding returnees to Sri Lanka has compiled a list of current risk profiles: (a) Individuals who are, or are perceived to be, a threat to the integrity of Sri Lanka as a single state because they are, or are perceived to have a significant role in relation to post-conflict Tamil separatism within the Diaspora and/or a renewal of hostilities within Sri Lanka.11 (b) Journalists (whether in print or other media) or human rights activists, who, in either case, have criticised the Sri Lankan government, in particular its human rights record, or who are associated with publications critical of the Sri Lankan government.12 (c) Individuals who have given evidence to the Lessons Learned and Reconciliation Commission implicating the Sri Lankan security forces, armed forces or the Sri Lankan authorities in alleged war crimes. Among those who may have witnessed war crimes during the conflict, particularly in the No-Fire Zones in May 2009, only those who have already identified themselves by giving such evidence would be known to the Sri Lankan authorities and therefore only they are at real risk of adverse attention or persecution on return as potential or actual war crimes witnesses.13 (d) A person whose name appears on a computerised "stop" list accessible at the airport, comprising a list of those against whom there is an extant court order or arrest warrant. Individuals whose name appears on a "stop" list will be stopped at the airport and handed over to the appropriate Sri Lankan authorities, in pursuance of such order or warrant. 14

The claimant has not participated or been involved in any anti-regime or pro-LTTE activities, either in Sri Lanka or since his arrival in Canada, and there is no evidence to indicate that the claimant would fit any of the current risk profiles. The panel, therefore, concludes that the claimant is unlikely to face any additional scrutiny upon his return to Sri Lanka as a result of his activities while in Sri Lanka and subsequent to his departure from Sri Lanka.

The panel has also considered the evidence regarding failed asylum-seekers, in light of the particular circumstances of this claimant and the risk profiles in the UNHCR guidelines. In light of this information, the panel finds that the claimant is not, on a balance of probabilities, a person who would be perceived to be linked to any pro-LTTE factions by the Sri Lankan government, and determines that he does not have good grounds to fear persecution as a failed asylum-seeker were he to be returned to Sri Lanka. The panel further finds that there is no evidence to suggest that since he fled Sri Lanka, the Sri Lankan government has any reason to believe he is a member or supporter of the LTTE. As already referenced, the Report from the United Kingdom Border Agency states that: The focus of the Sri Lankan government's concern has changed since the civil war ended in May 2009. The LTTE in Sri Lanka itself is a spent force and there have been no terrorist incidents since the end of the civil war. The government's present objective is to identify Tamil activists in the Diaspora who are working for Tamil separatism and to destabilise the unitary Sri Lankan state enshrined in Amendment 6(1) to the Sri Lankan Constitution in 1983, which prohibits the "violation of territorial integrity" of Sri Lanka. 15

The panel finds that with respect to reform and addressing the human rights abuses of the past, there is progress, albeit slow. At the same time, the panel acknowledges that problems with government security forces continue to exist. As highlighted in the UK Home Office Report: Since the country guidance case of GJ & Others was handed down in 2013, a new government, led by President Maithripala Sirisena came to office in January 2015. Following this, there have been positive developments including: curtailing of executive power; the reestablishment of independent commissions (and in particular the restoration of the legitimacy and independence of Sri Lanka's Human Rights Commission).16 The 'white van' abductions that operated outside all norms of law and order... are now very seldom reported. The number of torture complaints has reduced but new cases [of Tamil victims] continue to emerge... and police all too often continue to violence and excessive force.17 CONCLUSION

After careful consideration of all of the evidence, including the claimant's testimony, as well as submissions by the claimant's counsel, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on Convention grounds, or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be subject personally to a danger of torture, or face a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, if he were returned to Sri Lanka.

The panel therefore concludes that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection and rejects his claim.
